That the assault was carried out with the intent to attempt to commit the sexual assault. And so we know that there was a sexual assault because the defendant's semen and was found in the victim's anus and vagina, the amount of injury to the victim. I think that while we don't have a video, obviously, of the event, and we don't have a video in most of these types of events, there's more than sufficient evidence for a rational juror to conclude that the defendant's goal in mauling the victim was to accomplish the sexual act or to cover up the sexual act. I think that the trial court here pointed out a large public policy reason for rejecting the Huttner ruling, in that the Huttner ruling really encourages defendants to kill their victims in order to avoid felony murder and felony homicide charges. Because where there's no video, there's no other proof. If the victim can't make the allegation, then the people are left with proving almost something that is almost impossible, especially where you have a crime scene that has, you know, the crime scene that the police were presented with in this situation. So we know that an assault occurred, and we know that, I think counsel's brief points out the idea that maybe this assault occurred the sexual assault occurred after, based on the lack of information from family members stating that they didn't hear anything. Therefore the sexual assault occurred after the homicide. But I think that that's illogical as well because the homicide is by far the most destructive element on the biological functions of the victim. There was no sound for that as well. So I think that that cuts neutrally across for the people's case. I would encourage this court to not put the Hutner place in effect. This is not the case for it in any sense. We do not have a bright line event where the defendant killed a victim and then acknowledged the death of the individual and then raped a corpse. We have by all accounts, the evidence points to a blending of the events, why the defendant went into that room. And we also have the strong public policy argument that the law should not reward a defendant for killing their victim in order to avoid more serious charges. So moving on to the burglary aspect, which we addressed briefly. And then if the court upholds the burglary conviction or upholds any of the criminal sexual conduct convictions, the people agree that the Aguirre decision requires vacating all of the arising under. There can only be one unit of prosecution. And if the court determines that the CSCs should be vacated, then the court looks to the burglary. If it upholds the burglary decision, that should be remanded to the trial court to look at the other underlying cases for determination of that which should be vacated and that which should remain. The problem with defense counsel's idea that the prosecution has to put forth one theory of one case is double jeopardy. The problem there being that if we allege first degree criminal, that the defendant committed first degree criminal sexual conduct as the underlying crime, and then we don't allege third degree criminal sexual conduct as well. And if it doesn't go before the jury for determination as a lesser included offense, we will be barred from bringing that claim again if the defendant is acquitted on the more serious charge. Double jeopardy would attach since the lesser included offense necessarily contains the elements of the superior offense. So the people are really put in a rock and a hard place when we have to choose. I don't believe that Guam law requires us to plead out specific instances in these cases. There is a determination needs to be made by the trial court of which claims should be vacated. And that's going to be based upon whether or not this court sustains the burglary conviction and whether or not this court sustains the CSC convictions as well. That should be remanded to the trial court for consideration. And now turning my attention to the confession aspect, this issue was taken up. And I think that by the trial court and given extensive consideration for whether or not Mr. Acosta's will was overborne by the interviewing detectives. The great weight of the case law taking this issue up, and apparently this has happened multiple times in other jurisdictions around the United States, is that the officers have to weaponize, my word, weaponize religion in order for that religious conversation to overbore or overbear the will of the defendant to keep from making a statement to the officers. There is nothing in the record that indicates that the officer was not doing anything but having a genuine religious conversation with the defendant. The defendant filed an affidavit in support of his motion to suppress. And the affidavit does not contradict aspects of the officer's report, which the defendant had access to at the time that the affidavit was put together. There was no follow-up argument after the hearing on this issue where both detectives Mondia and Santos testified. Defendant did not follow up that hearing by alleging that any of the statements the officer made or any either officer made during that hearing were factually incorrect. Essentially, the defendant says what the officer said happened, happened, but it was so that the conversation was of such a nature that my will was overbore. That's a very self-serving statement by defendant after the fact. And I think that it would be a great risk if the court were to determine or just base it upon him stating later, boy, I really, really didn't mean to make that confession if the officers hadn't talked to me the way that they did, then I never would have told them what I told them. If that is sufficient on its face, then every defendant who makes a confession based upon any type of interaction with an officer is going to be able to have their statements suppressed based on saying, I wouldn't have said that had the officer not treated me the way that they treated me. And in this case, we don't have an issue with the officer treating the defendant, threatening the defendant. We don't have an issue with the officers depriving the defendant of sleep, depriving the defendant of food, depriving the defendant of bathroom breaks, depriving the defendant of cigarette breaks. We don't have an instance here where the officers misrepresented the defendant's rights. His Miranda rights were read to him multiple times. And we don't have an instance where the officer weaponized his sincere religious beliefs, and there's no contention that they were not sincere against the defendant. At no time is there an allegation that Officer Santos indicated that if the defendant didn't confess, he would go to hell or that he would suffer the, I guess, the persecution of God or another religious entity. That the officer openly discussed his sincere religious beliefs with the defendant should not be a basis for determining that the defendant's will was overborne. That the officer displayed a religious symbol or a religious phrase in his, and again, this was not done in an interrogation room. The evidence was that the officers brought Mr. Acosta back to the Criminal Investigation Division's office, uncuffed him, and then conducted this series of conversations with him. They spoke to him as officers are trained to develop rapport with a defendant. Rapport is far more likely to result in a confession than violence or force, and that is why modern officer training focuses on developing rapport with a suspect in a criminal case, and that is exactly what these officers did here. They treated him with respect. The defendant initiated conversation with Officer Santos about the death of his son. The defendant asked Officer Santos what he thought of the meaning of the biblical phrase that was on his board. Officer Santos responded to that. I think it would be unreasonable if the court expected Officer Santos to look at the defendant and say, I can't talk to you about that because there are restrictions on my ability to discuss religious ideology with you, especially my own ideology based upon the Supreme Court's decisions. I think that's an unrealistic requirement for police officers working in the field. And where does that stop if we prevent officers from sincerely discussing religious beliefs with suspects in criminal cases when they are prompted by the suspect? How about just general morality? Does it stop it there? It's a slippery slope. And so that's why all the cases that have taken this up, all the cases that we cite to, that have taken this up and looked at this issue, the majority have said that the relevant determination is whether or not the nature of the conversation, given the totality of the circumstances, was such that it was so coercive that it overbore the defendant's will. I don't have the statement right in front of me or the citation, but at least one court has pointed out that coerciveness in police interrogations is the goal. Every police interrogation has a degree of coerciveness baked into it. It is the goal of the officer to elicit an incriminating statement from the suspect. The question is not whether the officer's intent was coercive. The question is whether or not the officer's mechanism in eliciting the statement was so overbearing that the defendant felt that he did not have a choice in making the statement. And I do not believe that the facts in this case, which are what the court has to go on here, support that contention. We do agree with defense counsel that the trial court should take up the issue of determining whether the defendant has the ability to pay the fine that was imposed upon him. So this case should be remanded, at the very least, at the trial court for that hearing, which is statutorily mandated. However, we do not believe, and just to sum up the people's argument here in closing, that the court committed error in the recitation of the burglary instruction. We believe that the court has, the court followed this court's dictates in the Dimapon ruling, which only required, again, at least one of the, that the jury, that the totality of the instructions, the jury was adequately instructed that they had to make a finding that the defendant desired certain criminal consequences or objectively desired a specific result to follow his act. Under that reading, under the Dimapon language, the court did not, in reality, have to give the jury specific charges from which they could determine that the defendant had specific intent when he entered into the domicile of the victim in this case. The court could have let the jury determine any crime under the language of Dimapon, but the court did not. It told the jury, it specifically told the jury, you all have to be unanimous on the decision and you can only choose from the crimes that are set forth in the indictment and those crimes that are alleged.
